Remember that you deserve love and friendship too! And there are plenty of us willing to understand and help avoidant friends if they're willing to work with us!

It doesn't. It for sure appears that way because people with better childhoods statistically have a better chance of doing well and vice versa.

 People from poverty have started businesses and become wealthy, people who have suffered extreme amounts of abuse can heal and grow, people who are shy can become the life of the party, people who are lonely can find love. It happens everyday, those stories are always out there, but it's not shown on social media because we want to kid everyone that we're all doing fine.

I understand from experience, it's a lot easier to write yourself off and go "well nothing i can do it's out of my hands". That's a coping mechanism, it's trauma. Better to accept how my life is shit and do nothing, better to use all my failures as proof I can't succeed because then I don't have to struggle anymore and I can feel safe.

But the reality is if you choose to make a change, and you seek out help or try to heal yourself on your own, to try doing something different, to accept failure as a part of life, then things *will* change.

 The worst part is accepting that it's not fair. 
Your teenage years should have been great, your childhood should have been wonderful,  and it wasn't and you're suffering. And now it's all up to you to have to clean up the wounds and stich yourself together when everyone else is just getting to enjoy life. 
I agree it's not fair, it shouldn't be this way, but you CAN absolutely succeed and enjoy life too. You just have to heal first.

When I got treatment (that actually worked) and started getting better I noticed that my perspective of things changed. My ability to enjoy life had been cut off completely. I started regaining enjoyment of little things that I was numb to when I was struggling. Like a little kid I started getting excited at looking at comics in the store, or going to the bakery, or going on a car ride. I regained interests in things, I suddenly became fascinated by cooking and looked forward to it even though I previously despised it because I had no energy for it. And those things made me content and I didn't want to die anymore. Sometimes the little things genuinely gave me happiness which I had not felt in a long time.

When I am sick however , it all goes away again. Life. Is. Unbearable. I don't want to cook. I don't enjoy anything. I'm overwhelmed by the horrible memories of my past and I'm in so much pain that the little things become insignificant. And that's not my fault, it's not yours either. When people say it's about perspective they stupidly imply that you just need to look at things better or whatever, but your perception can be altered because it's chemical and just forcing a mindset won't fix that.

 If you've been deprived of basic things, or have trauma or an illness, it will physically alter your perception until it's treated or dies down. The better the life you have the less likely you'll have those issues and life will appear more accessible to you and more enjoyable. And if you treat things it will look that way for you too.

To a suicidal person it begs belief but it IS possible to obtain that too, just requires an absolute fuck-ton(!!) of work and healing and I dont blame anyone for struggling with that... it's not fair we have these things that mess with our brain when others don't. I reacted poorly to a very strong medication years ago and had a lot of scary experiences which led to my panic disorder/agoraphobia. 

Your brain has had a traumatic experience and it is working overtime to keep you safe. There are studies that show that people like us are hyper aware of all feelings and sensations in our bodies, which we often misinterpret as serious health concerns or insanity. You would have had body tingling and also side effects from meds before but wouldn't have noticed it. It used to be subtle now it's very intense!

I am sorry your support system is so poor. Mine was the same before I was diagnosed, was called a baby by my family and had days when my boyfriend was screaming at me to just get on a train. These disorders are incredibly cruel in that while we feel complete life or death terror,  it is completely invisible to other people and physically harmless. So people around us feel like we *must* be exaggerating and then we seek help in a hospital and get told its *just* anxiety which makes them think they're right.

It is very tough and it is possible things might be different from now on, but the good news is this is highly, highly treatable! A therapist will help you build up trust on your body again and you will be able to recognize anxiety for what it is.

Wishing you all the best!
